title: Counting blessings
hookLine: Emmons and McCullough (2003) found weekly gratitude lists brought small lifts in wellbeing

cards: Count your blessings. Grandmothers say it, usually across a kitchen table. There's an old gospel hymn with that title from 1897.
It's said so often it can sound like a way of telling someone to stop complaining. So in the early 2000s, two psychologists decided to find out whether it actually does anything.
They took the grandmother's advice and put it into a study with a control group.

teach.b: They were Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough, and their 2003 paper was called Counting Blessings Versus Burdens. In the first study, college students were split into three groups.
Once a week, for ten weeks, one group wrote down up to five things they were grateful for.
A second wrote five hassles, the irritations of the week. A third simply wrote five events that had affected them.

At the end, the gratitude group felt better about their lives as a whole and more hopeful about the week ahead, and they reported fewer physical complaints. They even said they'd spent more time exercising.

Later studies in the same paper, including one with people living with neuromuscular disease, found similar small lifts. That word small matters: modest changes, not transformations. What's interesting is the comparison.
Nobody gave the hassles group harder weeks; they just spent their attention on the burdens. The gratitude group spent the same few minutes on the blessings. Same life, same week, different count.
The grandmother was right about one thing and wrong about another. Counting doesn't make problems go away.

teach.h: WHAT YOU COUNT IS WHAT YOU NOTICE.
teach.b: But what you count is what you notice, and what you notice starts to shape the story you tell about your life.
And the first study was weekly, not daily: a few minutes once a week was enough to show a difference.

how: Some therapists and wellbeing courses use gratitude lists, often a few things written once a week, drawing in part on Emmons and McCullough's 2003 studies.

games.q: three groups each spend a few minutes a week writing. one counts blessings, one counts hassles, one lists events. which group feels better about life after ten weeks?

all three feel exactly the same.
games.why: the blessings group: better about life, more hopeful, fewer complaints. small lifts, from the same few minutes spent on a different count.

practice: Look back over the last seven days, not just today, and find one thing you're grateful for: a person, a meal, a moment of rest, something that didn't go wrong. Hold it for a breath, then find a second, a third, up to five.
If you get stuck, that's fine; stay with the ones you found, and breathe with the list.

wordCard.voice: Counting blessings. A weekly list of what you're grateful for, which brought small lifts in wellbeing in the Emmons and McCullough studies. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: count them. The grandmother had a point, if not the whole point. See you tomorrow.
